desaturated olive-green grade, the same organic 35mm film
grain. The first frame of this extension is identical to the
source video's last frame and the action flows on without a
pause or a cut.

The whole 30 seconds are ONE single continuous handheld take.
Every change of framing is reached PHYSICALLY: the camera
orbits, retreats, settles — always through space, always on
screen. There is NO cut, NO jump, NO new angle that the camera
did not travel to. An instant change of framing at any moment =
a failed take.

the whole shot. No door is opened, no door is used; nobody
walks out, nobody enters. The husband stays in the room to the
very last frame, facing the bed. A person leaving the room, a
door opening = a failed take.

The reference images tell you what the room and the people look
like. They are NOT framings, NOT camera positions, NOT moments
of this shot.

ceiling in old dark oak, sunk in half-darkness — the bed on the
LEFT seen from its foot end, freestanding, the tall headboard
deeper in the room; the stools with the copper basin by the
LEFT wall; the table with the white cloth, the low chest and
the small crucifix on the BACK wall; ONE modest two-leaf window
with a deep sill in the RIGHT wall, one soft pool of grey
daylight on the floorboards; a candle at the bed head, another
on the back table. It controls geometry, materials, light and
atmosphere ONLY — not framing.

linen shirt with full sleeves, olive green-brown wool
waistcoat, white neckcloth.

<<<image_4>>> is his WIFE, about twenty-five: narrow face, delicate

newborn in his arms, are the only people in the shot.

with a few dim spots, but still clearly REFLECTING the room;

panelling running into the corner where the window wall begins.

background of the frame behind him, dim and soft at first, and
it GROWS steadily nearer and sharper as he backs toward it
through the shot, until his back meets the EMPTY PANELLING

same panelling, the same light as <<<image_1>>> — never a new
location, never a different room, never a cut to elsewhere.

This shot is fast, breathless and alive. The camera works at running and
striding speed, whipping, swerving, pushing — it never coasts and never
drifts lazily. No beat is allowed to breathe, nothing is held, nothing is
contemplated: each event begins before the previous one has finished, so
the action overlaps and tumbles forward without a single lull. The crowd
churns, bodies cross the lens constantly, everything in the frame is in
motion at all times, and the camera keeps its energy all the way to the
final frame.

=== SPEED — CONSTANT REAL TIME ===
The whole video plays at one single constant real-time speed, from the
first frame to the last: 24 frames per second, normal playback, the same
rate throughout. No slow motion at any moment, no speed ramping, no time
remapping, no stretched or dragged moments.

=== THE CAMERA NEVER STOPS — IT ALWAYS HAS A LEADER ===
The camera is in motion in every single frame. It never holds, never
pauses, never settles into a locked frame, never hovers, never waits, and
it never travels on its own: in every moment it is FOLLOWING something that
moves — the dog, then the rolling cart, then the walking mourners, then the
running children — and when one leader leaves, the next one is already
moving inside the frame in the same instant. It is still moving when the
video ends: the final frame is caught mid-move, as if the shot continues
past the end of the file. Nothing ever waits for anything: the camera does
not wait for a subject, and no person or animal waits for the camera. Every
action is already under way when the camera reaches it.

=== NOTHING APPEARS OUT OF THIN AIR ===
Every creature and object enters the frame by physically travelling in from
outside the frame edge, in full motion, already running or moving before it
becomes visible. Nothing fades in, nothing materialises, nothing pops into
existence inside the frame.

=== THE WORLD ===
The same narrow cobblestone market street as in the source video: a
decaying Central European city in the 1780s, early morning, and the market
is heaving — the street is packed wall to wall, bodies shoulder to
shoulder, overlapping and layered from the foreground into the far haze,
only patches of wet cobblestone showing between the legs. The crowd streams
in both directions: market women in dirty linen caps, porters bent under
sacks and rolling barrels, customers haggling at every stall, a
water-carrier with a wooden yoke, barefoot children darting through gaps,
chickens and pigs underfoot, stray dogs, hand-barrows pushed through the
press. Three-storey townhouses with flaking plaster and soot streaks, dark
sagging canvas awnings over wooden stalls, wrought-iron guild signs, deep
dark stone gateways, laundry lines above, chimney smoke rising into a flat
pale sky. A shallow open gutter with a faint red-pink trace runs down the
street. Everything in frame belongs to the 1780s: no modern object, no
plastic, no electric light.

Moving through this crowd: a tired horse draws a plain flat wooden cart at
a steady walking pace, the cart always rolling, its wheels always turning,
the crowd parting around it and closing again behind it. On the flat boards
lies a simple coffin of dark wood — plain boards stained almost black, with
a dull matte surface and no ornament, the grain just visible under the
stain. Following directly behind the rolling cart and moving with it in the
same direction, a few steps back, walks an old priest: a stooped elderly
man in a long dark cassock worn grey-black with age, a dark cloak over his
shoulders, thin white hair, holding a worn black prayer book against his
chest, his lips moving. Behind him, walking in the same direction and
keeping the same pace, come three old mourning women in dark shawls and
white linen caps, each one a clearly different woman — one broad and
strong, one tiny and bent over a stick — never copies of each other. The
woman of <<<image_1>>> is among them, nearest the camera, and there is only one
of her: the man in that coffin was her husband, and she is breaking down as
she walks, held up under the arm by the broad one beside her. The priest
and the women stay together behind the cart for the whole time they are in
frame, following it, never overtaking it and never turning back toward it.

A narrow side lane opens off the market street: quieter than the main
street but far from empty, a working back lane of the poor. Washing lines
sag from wall to wall above it, hung with grey linen. Deep in the lane two
washerwomen work at a long wooden trough by a stone well, sleeves rolled,
steam rising off the water, wringing cloth and slapping it down. A woman
leans out of a low doorway and empties a wooden pail of slops into the
gutter. An old man sits on a step mending a wicker basket on his knees. A
lean cat picks its way along a wall. People keep walking through: a woman
with a bundle of firewood on her back, a man rolling a barrel, a boy with a
jug. Everyone passes without stopping and nobody looks at the woman sitting
there.

And in that lane, on her own stone step: a young mother, worn down by
hard living, sitting alone — her simple light linen summer dress faded to
pale dusty blue-grey, smudged with dirt and ash, the hem caked with dried
mud, a small tear at the shoulder seam; her head uncovered, hair half
fallen out of its pins, loose greasy strands around a tired young face,
grime on her cheek and hands. She is nursing her baby: the infant is
loosely half-covered by a plain stained linen cloth across its middle — the
top of its small head, one bare leg and a tiny bare foot stay visible; the
mother's curved body, her bowed head and the cloth keep the nursing itself
completely hidden at all times.

=== CAMERA — FIVE HAND-OFFS, ONE FLIGHT ===
One camera, 50mm lens, fluid and fast, in continuous motion, always carried
by whatever moves inside the frame. The whole take is one flight built of
five hand-offs, and at every hand-off the new leader is ALREADY VISIBLE and
ALREADY MOVING in the frame while the old leader is still there:

Hand-off 1 — dog to rolling cart: the dog runs toward the moving cart,
which is already rolling across the frame in profile ahead of it; when the
dog dives under the turning wheels, the camera is already rising alongside
the cart.
Hand-off 2 — coffin to mourners: the camera travels along the length of the
coffin seen in profile, and as the far end of the coffin slides out of
frame it uncovers the mourners walking right behind the cart in the same
direction — first the old priest, then the three women — all of them
already in motion, already following the cart; the camera settles into
their pace and travels alongside them, holding them in profile as they
walk.
Hand-off 3 — mourning woman to couple: while the camera moves with the
walking old woman and pushes in on her crying face, the kissing couple is
already visible deep behind her in the gateway; the camera slips past her
shoulder and the same push carries on to the couple.
Hand-off 4 — couple to boy: while the camera circles slowly around the
couple, never stopping, the barefoot boy is already creeping into the frame
from the right; the theft happens inside the same moving frame that holds
the couple, and the boy's explosive sprint gives the camera its next
leader.
Hand-off 5 — children to seated woman: while the children are still running
down the lane, the seated woman is already visible at its corner; the
camera lets the children go and lands its motion on her, still advancing.

Framing rule for the whole take: the main subject — the point where the
viewer's eye is meant to rest — is NEVER in the centre of the frame. It
always sits on the left third or the right third, and the crowded street
opens into the remaining two thirds. Never a symmetrical corridor down the
street axis. Shallow depth of field, the near subject razor sharp, the
crowded depth soft, bright and hazy.

=== ACTION — ONE UNBROKEN FLOW, 25 SECONDS ===

porter's legs sweep across the near foreground and wipe the frame — and
behind them the wooden cart is already rolling across the shot IN PROFILE,

the flat boards.
6-15s: The camera now travels along the side of the rolling cart, moving
down the full length of the plain dark coffin seen in profile — its
near-black stained boards, its rough joints, its worn edges catching only a
faint dull sheen as they slide past the lens in the same direction the cart
is going. A woman with a basket on her hip crosses the near foreground and
wipes the frame. As the far end of the coffin slides out of shot it
uncovers the mourners following right behind the cart, all moving the same

the black prayer book held to his chest, his lips moving as he walks — and
a few steps behind him the three old mourning women in dark shawls and
white linen caps, their skirts swinging with their steps. The camera
travels alongside them at their pace and holds on the nearest woman, her
old creased face on the right third of the frame: this is her husband on
the cart, and she is coming apart. Her whole body sobs — her shoulders jerk
with each breath, her chest heaves, her breath catches and tears out of her
in ragged gasps, her mouth opens and twists, her chin shakes. Tears run
down the deep creases beside her nose into her collar. She drags the back
of her wrist across her eyes and it does not help. Her knees go loose for a
step and the woman beside her grips her under the arm and holds her up, and
they keep walking. Deep behind her shoulder, in a dark stone gateway, the
kissing couple is already visible, soft and out of focus.
15-20s: Without pausing, the camera slips past her moving shoulder and the
same push carries on, the old woman sliding out of frame; a man carrying a
stack of crates crosses the foreground and wipes the frame, and the couple
comes through in the shadow of their gateway, held in an American shot from
the knees up on the left third and never framed any closer: deep in the
dark recess, wrapped in each other and kissing without pause, in constant
soft motion — his hand sliding up her back, her fingers closing in his

locked on the bag, ducking under a passing porter's sack. He slides his
small hand under the loose flap, draws out a small leather purse in one
smooth silent pull — and EXPLODES into a sprint to the left, the purse
clutched to his chest. The couple never notices, and never stops kissing.
The camera whips left with the boy, catching him in clean side profile, and
two more ragged street boys peel off the wall and run with him — different
ages, different hair, different rags, no two alike.
20-25s: The three boys race in profile through the heaving crowd at full

the RIGHT into a narrow side lane and the camera bends in behind them,
chasing their backs down a lane that is busy with its own life: washing
lines sagging overhead, two washerwomen working at a trough by the well in

boys rush past her, an old man on a step mending a basket who does not even
look up, a cat bolting along the wall away from the running feet. And at
the corner of the lane, on her stone step, the young mother is already
visible on the left third of the frame, sitting with her back curved
forward and her head bowed low over the small child held close in both her

=== THE WORLD ===
A narrow cobblestone market street in a decaying Central European city in
the 1780s, early morning, the market in full swing and packed with people.
Three-storey townhouses wall to wall, flaking lime plaster over old brick,
soot streaks, dark sagging canvas awnings over wooden stalls on both sides,
wrought-iron guild signs, deep dark gateways, laundry lines above. A shallow
open gutter runs down the middle of the street carrying dirty water, fish
scales, straw and a faint red-pink trace from the fish stalls. Mud, straw,
spilled grain and puddles between uneven cobbles; stacked crates, barrels
and wicker baskets crowd the base of every stall. The crowd fills the
street: market women in dirty linen caps, porters with sacks and barrels, a
water-carrier with a wooden yoke, customers haggling at every stall,
barefoot children, chickens and pigs underfoot, lean stray dogs slipping
between the legs of the crowd, hand-carts and a tired cart horse. Everything
in frame belongs to the 1780s: no modern object, no plastic, no electric
light.

The fish stall at the end of this shot has a small, low, narrow butchering
table standing at its front edge, facing the street: a scarred wooden
chopping board sits right at the very edge of that table, so that whatever
lies on the board is only a short jump above the heads of the dogs moving
through the crowd below.

=== CAMERA — HOW IT MOVES ===
One camera, 50mm lens, fluid and fast, in continuous motion. This is an
impossible camera: it flies at the height of a rat, races along the wet
cobbles, dives under carts, squeezes between wheel spokes and stall legs,
cuts through the forest of moving human legs, swerves around baskets and
barrels, climbs a stall, and finally drops back down into the street after a
running dog — a move no real camera operator could perform, executed as one
smooth unbroken flight.

The camera changes its type of movement four times, and each change is
caused by a new subject taking over the shot:
First movement — a low PUSH IN: the camera glides forward along the
cobblestones behind the rolling spindle, travelling deeper into the street,
following the unspooling thread away from the lens.
Second movement — a DOLLY RIGHT: when the rat runs in from the left edge of
frame, the camera stops pushing forward and instead tracks sideways to the
right, moving parallel to the rat, holding it in clean full side profile as
it runs, the street sliding past behind it. From there the camera stays with
the animal through the chase, swerving, diving and rolling with every change
of direction.
Third movement — a CLIMB and a SLOW EASE: the camera rises vertically up the
stall leg, crests the butchering table, and gradually decelerates into a
slow gentle forward drift toward the working hands, without ever coming to a
stop.
Fourth movement — a DROP and a CHASE: when the dog snatches the fish head
the camera whips down off the table after it and races low through the crowd
behind the running dog, accelerating as the video ends.

Framing rule for the whole take: the subject is never centred. It sits on
the left or right third while the crowded street opens into the rest of the
frame. Never a symmetrical corridor down the street axis. Foreground
occlusion is constant: skirts, boots, wheel spokes, basket rims, straw and
stall legs sweep through the near foreground out of focus, wiping the lens
and revealing the sharp subject behind. Shallow depth of field, the near
subject razor sharp, the crowded depth soft, bright and hazy.

=== ACTION — ONE UNBROKEN FLOW ===
0-3s: The camera is already moving in a low push in, gliding forward just
above the wet cobbles among the moving feet of the crowd. A wooden spindle
wound with pale ecru linen thread rolls fast across the stones ahead of the
lens, its thin thread unspooling behind it. The camera pushes after it, low
and close, boots and skirts sweeping past out of focus.
3-6s: The spindle strikes the raised stone lip of the open gutter and stops
dead. In that same instant a large grey-brown rat with wet fur RUNS INTO THE
FRAME FROM THE LEFT EDGE, already at full speed, and crosses in front of the
camera. The camera abandons the spindle, stops pushing forward and swings
into a sideways dolly right, travelling parallel to the running rat and
holding it in clean full side profile on the left third of the frame, its
legs working, tail streaming behind. The rat leaps the gutter in one bound,
splashing water, still in profile.
6-10s: The rat cuts into the crowd. It sprints between moving boots and
wooden clogs, dives beneath a standing hand-cart — the camera diving with
it, sliding under the axle between the turning wheel spokes, straw and mud
flying past the lens — and bursts out the other side.
10-14s: The rat runs the length of a fallen barrel, leaps down into spilled
grain that sprays up around it, and threads at speed through a row of wicker
baskets and stacked crates, the camera swerving and rolling with every
change of direction. A startled chicken scatters across the frame in a burst
of wings.
14-17s: Without slowing, the rat reaches the fish stall and is already
climbing the rough wooden leg, claws sunk into the split grain. The camera
races up with it out of the mud, past straw and baskets, into the shade
beneath the sagging canvas awning, the wooden leg sliding down through
frame. As the camera crests the boards the rat slips away between the
stacked baskets at the back of the stall and is gone from the frame.
17-21s: The camera crests the small low butchering table at the front edge
of the stall and eases into a slow gentle forward glide. The fishwife's work
is already under way as the camera arrives: her reddened left hand holds a
large silver river fish flat on the scarred board and her heavy dark iron
cleaver is ALREADY FALLING, halfway through its swing. The blade lands once,
hard and clean, just behind the gills, and severs only the head from the
body. That is the only cleaver blow in this video: one single chop, and the
blade stays down in the board afterwards. The severed head lies on the board
at the very edge of the table; the body of the fish stays whole and
unbroken beside it, one single complete fish body, never split, never cut
into pieces. Scales and droplets fly up around the blade.
21-25s: In the same second, from below and out of nowhere, a lean stray dog
launches up from the crowd, its front paws hitting the edge of the table,
and snatches the severed fish head off the board in its jaws. It twists in
mid-air and drops back into the street, already running. The fishwife's arm
swings after it a beat too late, missing. The camera whips down off the
table after the dog and races low behind it through the forest of moving
legs, mud and straw flying past the lens, the dog carrying the fish head
away into the crowd, still accelerating as the video ends in full motion.

One single light source for the whole video: a soft, fully diffuse overcast
morning sky, scattered through haze and chimney smoke so it arrives from
everywhere at once and casts no hard shadows anywhere. No direct sun, no
sunbeam, no golden light, no sunrise warmth, no artificial film lighting, no
rim light. The light is cold, milky and grey-blue and falls evenly from
above. The depth of the street is always the brightest part of the frame:
pale milky grey-green haze glowing between the buildings, distant people
reading as soft dark silhouettes against it, while the near foreground and
the ground under the awnings sit a stop darker. The only warm light comes
from real flames inside the frame: one or two small oil lanterns.

percent cold grey-green: wet stone, mud, plaster, shadow. Thirty percent
weathered brown and dirty off-white: old wood, wicker, canvas, dirty linen
clothing and caps. Ten percent the only saturated notes: the faint red-pink
of the gutter water, the fresh red of the cut fish, the small amber flame of
a lantern. Silver fish scales and white linen caps are the bright
counter-note. Highlights milky and slightly cyan; shadows dense, green-brown
and detailed, never crushed to pure black.

Photorealistic 35mm motion-picture film, Kodak Vision3 250D stock,
photochemical colour, organic film grain thickening in the shadows, soft
highlight roll-off, gentle optical falloff toward the frame edges, natural
motion blur at 24 frames per second, real motion blur on every fast move.

for one heartbeat only — mid-work, a cloth in her hand — and
says, calmer, almost kind:
"Sir — see to the child. Let us work."
Then she is GONE to the bed, without another look, out of the
frame. She never stands idle, never waits.
14-25s: HE SHRINKS BACK. Alone with the answer that was not an
answer, he looks down at the crying child — one long look —
then up again. And he SHRINKS BACK from what he sees, the way a
man backs away from something terrifying he cannot stop
watching: slow, uncertain, blind backward steps — HIS HEELS
REACHING BACK, feeling for the floor behind him, his TOES
POINTING TOWARD THE CAMERA at every single step, his chest and
face SQUARE TO THE CAMERA the whole way, his eyes never leaving
the bed. Step by step his figure grows SMALLER in the standing
frame, the dim wall of <<<image_2>>> rising behind his shoulders,
the mirror sliding into view at his right — until, at about the
25th second, his back MEETS the empty dark panelling between
the mirror and the corner, and he stops, pressed against it.
He never turns around, never looks behind him, never glances at
the wall or the mirror.
25-30s: THE WALL AND THE MIRROR. As the camera walks its slow
push in: he stands pinned to the panelling, the crying child in
his now entirely red hands, his eyes fixed past the camera on
the bed. In the MIRROR at the right of the frame: the dim,
blurred, MOVING reflection of the women at the bed — bent
shapes, lifted linen, hurry — indistinct but alive. He does not
move. The wife's low moans keep coming at intervals under the
child's cry, to the very last frame. The shot ends there.

=== ACTING ===
THE MAN: rooted shock; one question with his whole heart in it;
then the backward shrinking of a man who cannot stop watching —
uncertain heels, stiff arms around the child, eyes locked
forward; at the wall, total silent open terror — eyes wide,
wet, fixed; no tears running, no sobbing, no shouting.
HANNAH: a woman in the middle of an emergency — her lines
thrown while moving, rough but never cruel; the second line the
practised half-comfort said over a shoulder. She NEVER stands
still waiting for him to speak.
THE WIFE: mostly sound — low guttural moans every few seconds,
each a little weaker, never stopping for long, to the last
frame. She never speaks.
THE MIDWIFE and JANE: at the bed, behind the camera and in the
mirror — fast hands, bent backs, silence.

=== SPEED ===
Natural real-time speed throughout. No slow motion anywhere.
The orbit smooth; the exchange QUICK — no dead air; his
backward steps SLOW and uncertain, reaching the wall around the
25th second; the final push in calm and even.

=== SINGULARITY ===
Exactly FIVE adults and ONE newborn child in the whole shot —
no one else, no extra figures, no figures in the mirror other
than the working women. There is only ever ONE bedroom — the
single room defined together by <<<image_1>>> and <<<image_2>>> — never a
second room, never a new space. Exactly ONE bundle, the child's
head visible at its top, in his arms to the end. Exactly ONE
mirror — and it IS in the final framing. Exactly ONE door —
CLOSED, never used, never reached for. The wife stays in the
bed. Whatever lies on the windowsill in the source video stays
exactly where it is, untouched. Nothing duplicated.

=== LOOK LOCK — THE SOURCE GRADE IS THE LAW ===
Every frame keeps the EXACT look of the source video and of
<<<image_1>>> and <<<image_2>>>: the same heavy desaturated olive-green
grade, the same milky cyan-leaning highlights, the same dense
green-brown shadows with detail, the same organic 35mm film
grain, the same low-key light. The red of the soaked cloth sits
INSIDE this grade — dark, desaturated, brown-leaning crimson,
never a bright saturated red. A cleaner, brighter, more
colourful or sharper digital look at any point = a failed take.

=== LIGHT ===
Low-key, exactly as in the source video and in both room
references: one soft pool of grey overcast daylight from the
single window — off at the side — and weak candle flames
glowing without lighting the room; the dark oak panelling
drinking the light. The wall of <<<image_2>>> is the DARKEST wall of
the room: his face there lit only by the far grey light, one
side falling into shadow; the mirror holds a dim grey gleam
with the moving reflection in it. NO light comes from the
camera: no fill, no glow lifting the faces — more darkness than
light on every face, small catch-lights in the eyes. A brightly
lit face, an evenly lit face or a brightly lit bed = a failed
take.

=== FILM ===
Photorealistic 35mm motion-picture film, Kodak Vision3 250D
stock, photochemical colour, organic film grain thickening in
the shadows, soft highlight roll-off, natural 24 fps motion
blur, gentle real handheld sway in the standing frame. 50mm
lens, natural depth: his face sharp, Hannah blurred when near
the lens, the mirror reflection softly blurred — never a creamy
wall of bokeh. Not a video game, not a 3D render, not a clean
digital look, no beauty light, no retouch. Real textures: damp
hair, sweat, unretouched skin with open pores, coarse linen and
wool, wet soaked crumpled linen, old waxed oak panelling, aged
hazy mirror glass.

=== AUDIO ===
Raw location sound only, no music anywhere. Through the WHOLE
shot, never stopping: <the newborn's cry, close against his
chest, rising and falling> and, every few seconds, <the wife's
low guttural moan of pain from the bed, each one a little
weaker>. 0-4s: under those, <the room: hurried linen, water,
quick feet behind the camera>. 4-14s: Hannah's two lines and
his one question — quick, no dead air — with <cloth and water
and hurried feet> under them. 14-25s: <his slow uncertain
backward steps on the worn floorboards, one by one, growing
quieter with distance> <his shallow breathing> <the work at the
bed behind the camera>. 25-30s: <his back meeting the
panelling, a soft wooden knock> — then only <the child's cry>
<his breathing> <the hurried work behind the camera> and <her
moans, to the last frame>. Apart from the three lines, not one
word is spoken.
